new_quiz.q: A material uses a normal Texture Sample node. What happens to the pattern when you scale the mesh up?
choices: The pattern keeps its size
The pattern stretches with the mesh
The pattern disappears
The pattern turns gray
new_quiz.explain: A normal Texture Sample follows the UVs of the mesh. When the mesh is scaled, the UVs are scaled too, so the pattern stretches.

new_quiz.q: How does world-aligned texturing place a texture?
choices: It paints the texture by hand on each mesh
It copies the UVs from another mesh
It projects the texture from the world, not from the UVs of the mesh
It bakes the texture into the lighting
new_quiz.explain: The texture is projected using positions in the world. The UVs of the mesh play no part, so their quality does not matter.

new_quiz.q: You apply a world-aligned material to three cubes of different sizes. What do you see?
choices: The pattern keeps the same size on all of them
The pattern is largest on the smallest cube
The pattern shows only on the largest cube
The pattern has a different color on each cube
new_quiz.explain: Because the texture is measured in world space, one tile has the same size everywhere. Scaling a mesh does not change it.

new_quiz.q: Which node projects a texture from the world in this quest?
choices: Texture Sample
Landscape Layer Blend
Constant3Vector
WorldAlignedTexture
new_quiz.explain: WorldAlignedTexture is the node that does the world projection. A normal Texture Sample node follows the UVs.

new_quiz.q: How do you give your texture to the WorldAlignedTexture node?
choices: Connect a Texture Object node to its TextureObject input
Connect a Constant node to its Base Color input
Type the name of the texture in its title
Drag the texture onto the mesh in the level
new_quiz.explain: The node needs the texture itself, not a sampled color. A Texture Object node holds the texture and connects to the TextureObject input.

new_quiz.q: Which output of the WorldAlignedTexture node do you connect to Base Color?
choices: TextureObject
Roughness
XYZ Texture
Emissive Color
new_quiz.explain: XYZ Texture is the result of the projection from all three axes. It covers every side of the mesh.

new_quiz.q: When is world-aligned texturing most useful?
choices: On characters that are animated
On blockout meshes whose UVs are not good enough yet
On meshes that never get a texture
On the sky of a level
new_quiz.explain: Blockout meshes are simple shapes for planning a level, and you scale them all the time. World-aligned texturing gives them a clean pattern with no UV work.

new_quiz.q: What happens to a world-aligned pattern when you move the mesh through the level?
choices: The pattern is deleted
The pattern moves with the mesh
The pattern becomes larger
The pattern stays fixed in the world, so it slides over the mesh
new_quiz.explain: The pattern belongs to the world and not to the mesh. That is fine for static blockout meshes, but it looks wrong on things that move.

new_quiz.q: What can a landscape material do with grass?
choices: Place grass meshes on every spot where one paint layer is painted
Draw grass as a flat color on the ground
Turn every mesh in the level into grass
Import grass meshes from Fab by itself
new_quiz.explain: The material can output grass for a paint layer. Wherever that layer is painted, the landscape places grass meshes.

new_quiz.q: Why let the landscape material place the grass?
choices: Grass placed by hand cannot be seen in the game
Grass placed by hand has no collision
Placing grass by hand over a large landscape takes a long time
Placing grass by hand needs a plugin
new_quiz.explain: A landscape can be very large. Grass that follows a painted layer saves the work of placing it by hand.

new_quiz.q: How do you create a Landscape Grass Type asset?
choices: Open Landscape Mode and choose New on the Manage tab
Right-click in the Content Browser, open Foliage and choose Landscape Grass Type
Open Edit, then Plugins, and enable Landscape Grass Type
Right-click in the Content Browser, open Miscellaneous and choose Data Asset
new_quiz.explain: Landscape Grass Type is in the Foliage group of the Content Browser menu. You then add a small mesh to the asset.

new_quiz.q: Which node in the landscape material sends grass to the landscape?
choices: Landscape Layer Blend
WorldAlignedTexture
Texture Sample
Landscape Grass Output
new_quiz.explain: The Landscape Grass Output node is where the material tells the landscape which grass to place and where.

new_quiz.q: Where do you pick your Landscape Grass Type asset on the Landscape Grass Output node?
choices: In the title of the node
In the Parameter Name of the node
Under Grass Types in the Details panel of the node
In the Stats panel of the Material Editor
new_quiz.explain: You select the node, add one element under Grass Types, and pick the asset there. The node then gets an input for that grass type.

new_quiz.q: What does the Landscape Layer Sample node give to the grass type input?
choices: The painted amount of one paint layer
The height of the landscape
The color of the grass mesh
The number of grass meshes
new_quiz.explain: The node reads how much of the named layer is painted at each spot. Connected to the grass type, it makes that layer control where the grass appears.

new_quiz.q: You painted the layer, but no grass appears. What do you check first on the Landscape Layer Sample node?
choices: That it is connected to Base Color
That its Parameter Name is the name of the paint layer
That it has a texture assigned
That it is placed left of all other nodes
new_quiz.explain: The node finds the layer by its name. If Parameter Name does not match the layer you paint, it reads nothing and no grass is placed.

new_quiz.q: How do you confirm that the setup works?
choices: Grass appears on the whole landscape
Grass appears only in the Material Editor preview
Grass appears only after you press Play
Grass appears only in the places where you painted the layer
new_quiz.explain: The grass must follow your painting. If it shows only where the layer is painted, the layer is driving the grass.

new_quiz.q: What is an emissive material?
choices: A material that is transparent
A material that reflects like a mirror
A material that glows
A material that is projected onto surfaces
new_quiz.explain: An emissive material gives off light of its own, like a screen, a sign or a lamp.

new_quiz.q: What is Lumen?
choices: The lighting system in Unreal Engine 5 that calculates bounced light
The unit in which Unreal measures color temperature
The editor where you build materials
A plugin that adds lakes and rivers
new_quiz.explain: Lumen calculates how light bounces between surfaces. This is what lets a glowing surface add light to the scene.

new_quiz.q: What can a glowing surface do when Lumen is on?
choices: It can replace the Post Process Volume
It can cast sharp shadows like the sun
It can turn off the other lights
It can light the things near it
new_quiz.explain: Lumen treats the glow as light that bounces into the scene. Surfaces near the screen pick up its color.

new_quiz.q: How do you build the glow in the material?
choices: Connect a color to Roughness
Multiply a color or a texture by the Scalar Parameter Intensity and connect the result to Emissive Color
Set the Material Domain to Deferred Decal
Connect the Scalar Parameter Intensity to Metallic
new_quiz.explain: The color or texture decides what glows, and Intensity decides how strong the glow is. Their product goes into Emissive Color.

new_quiz.q: Why do you make a Material Instance of the emissive material?
choices: So you can change how strong the glow is
So Lumen is turned on
So the material becomes a light actor
So the screen gets collision
new_quiz.explain: Intensity is a parameter, so an instance can change it quickly. You try the values 1, 10 and 50 and compare the results.

new_quiz.q: Why do you test the glow in a dark place, such as a closed room?
choices: Emissive materials do not work outdoors
Lumen is turned off in bright levels
The glow is easy to see there
Dark rooms need no material
new_quiz.explain: In a bright level the sun hides the small amount of light from the screen. In a dark room you see clearly what the glow adds.

new_quiz.q: What happens when you raise Intensity from 1 to 50?
choices: The glow changes its color to white only on the edges
The surface becomes transparent
The glow stays the same, but the room gets darker
The glow becomes much stronger and lights the nearby surfaces more
new_quiz.explain: Intensity multiplies the emissive color. A higher value sends more light into the scene.

new_quiz.q: When do you still need a real light next to an emissive surface?
choices: When the material has a parameter
When the glow does not give enough light for the scene
When the room has more than four walls
When Lumen is turned on
new_quiz.explain: A glowing surface does not always light its surroundings well enough. A real light then gives the light that the glow alone cannot.

new_quiz.q: Why do you walk through the scene at eye level?
choices: It makes the scene render faster
It shows problems that a still render hides
It creates the Material Instances
It paints the landscape layers
new_quiz.explain: Walking shows gaps, stretched textures and places where you get stuck. A single still picture can hide all of these.

new_quiz.q: Which three things make the scene walkable?
choices: A Sky Light, a Directional Light and Height Fog
A Cine Camera, a bookmark and a screenshot
A Player Start, collision on the meshes and no dead ends
A master material, an instance and a decal
new_quiz.explain: The Player Start puts the player in the scene. Collision keeps the player from walking through meshes, and a scene without dead ends can be walked all the way.

new_quiz.q: In Play In Editor you walk straight through a rock. What do you check first?
choices: That the rock mesh has collision
That the rock uses a Material Instance
That the rock has a decal
That the rock is on the landscape
new_quiz.explain: Without collision, a mesh is only a picture and nothing stops the player. The mesh needs collision to be solid.

new_quiz.q: Which parameters does M_Master_Surface have?
choices: Sun angle, fog color and exposure
Width, height and depth
Speed, health and score
Color, roughness, a texture and tiling
new_quiz.explain: These four parameters are enough to make many different surfaces from one graph. Each instance sets its own values.

new_quiz.q: How do at least 5 surfaces in the scene get their different looks?
choices: Each surface uses its own new material graph
Each surface uses an instance of the one master material
Each surface is painted in another program
Each surface uses a different landscape
new_quiz.explain: The instances share one graph and differ only in their parameter values. The scene stays easy to manage, because there is only one material to maintain.

new_quiz.q: What does the landscape material of the scene need?
choices: 3 layers and a Landscape Layer Blend node
3 lights and a Sky Atmosphere
1 layer and a WorldAlignedTexture node
5 instances and a decal
new_quiz.explain: The Landscape Layer Blend node mixes the 3 layers based on where you paint. You then paint the layers on the landscape.

new_quiz.q: What must each of the 3 decals in the scene have?
choices: A light of its own
A collision box
A name that starts with MI_
A purpose, such as a stain under a pipe or an arrow toward the path
new_quiz.explain: A decal should tell something about the place or guide the player. Decals placed without a reason only add noise.

new_quiz.q: What does your short note about the master material say?
choices: How long the scene took to build
Which plugins the project uses
Which parameters it has and what each one is for
Where the textures were downloaded
new_quiz.explain: The note lists the parameters and explains each one. Someone else can then make new instances without reading the graph.
